newsitem.title: UK: N.Sea crude markets start the week cautiously.
newsitem.headline: N.Sea crude markets start the week cautiously.

text.p: North Sea crude markets made a typically slow start on Monday after last week's spike in outright values on fears of hurricane damage in the Gulf of Mexico, traders said.
The realisation that Hurricane Danny would not hit oil production badly saw futures lose all of Thursday's gains and more on Friday, which led strong front-end cash spreads into a late dip.
Aug/Sept traded as high as +19 cents before slipping back to trade at +12 cents in the U.S. on Friday and the spread held its value in very limited discussion on Monday.
The spread was quoted at +0.05/+0.13 on Monday, with tightness in the prompt physical market allowing it to hold onto its backwardation.
Outright values at 11.40 gmt stood at $18.13 a barrel for September Brent, down just a cent, after Friday's 57 cent drop.
Production problems in the North Sea also helped the bullish tone in the prompt market.
Non-Brent grades were being talked up last week as buyers decided the relief Iraq's exports was supposed to bring to prices was too long coming.
"Its a mixture of waiting for news on Iraq, or deciding there is no news and deciding to get on with things," said one broker. "The mood in the market definetly swung towards the latter last week."

News that Iraq submitted its aid distribution plan to the U.N. on Monday, clearing another hurdle in the way of resumed crude sales, caused barely a ripple in the market with traders focused on short-term supply problems.
Sources at Enterprise Oil, operators of the troubled Nelson field, said they anticipated cutting production to under 50,000 barrels per day later in the week to allow repairs to proceed.

Production has already been throttled back from 140,000 to 110,000 bpd because of problems with gas equipment, with two cargoes from the July loading programme for the Forties system deferred to August as a result.

Saga Petroleum's 200,000 bpd Snorre oil field also reported problems, shutting in production from Sunday night because of a power failure that they did not forsee resolving until Tuesday at the earliest.
A Brent cargo traded 10 cents weaker on Friday, at five cents below August. But this was said to be a reflection of positions taken on the swaps market and the real value was several cents higher.

The real strength of demand for August barrels was underscored when all five Brent dates were kept ahead of the five o'clock deadline on Friday. There are no cargoes turning wet from the chains on Monday.
"I think we are going to see more of the CFD game by the big guys again today," said one broker, who anticipated a quiet physical market.
Bid/offer spreads for short-terms swaps broadened, with this week against bid at +2 cents, while offers were believed to be around +15 cents. Next week (July 28-01) was talked at -0.09/0.00.
An August 4-8/11-15 roll was heard done at +5 cents but otherwise activity was limited.
